\caption{(a) Relative count error $(\hat c-k)/k$ against requested repetitions

\subsection{Models undercount repetitions, proportionally}

Figure~\ref{fig:main}(a) shows the relative count error against $k$. Below
$k\!=\!6$ every model is essentially exact; above it, repeated items are rendered
with a median error of \ErrRepCk{}\% per checkpoint, or \ErrRep{}\%
$[\ErrRepLo{},\ErrRepHi{}]$ pooling items ($n=\ErrRepN{}$) --- pooling weights
checkpoints by surviving item count, so we quote both. Either way it is
one-directional: models produce \emph{fewer} repetitions than requested.

Within $k\le32$ that deficit is \emph{proportional}, not saturating --- not what
Theorem~\ref{thm:collapse}(iv) predicts. A constant fits the panel's median count
above $k\!=\!6$ with residual sum of squares \ShapeSatSSE{} against
\ShapePropSSE{} for $\hat c=\ShapePropSlope{}k$ (S10), so no horizon lies inside
this ladder.

\subsection{Past the ladder, the count does level off}

So we extended it, post hoc, to $k\in\{48,64,96,128\}$ on the \HzNModels{}
checkpoints that admit utterances that long (\HzModelNames{}; XTTS-v2's
$602$-mel-token ceiling censors every $k\ge48$ item, S10). Tracking stops: the
repeated median sits at \HzMedRepKLo{} and \HzMedRepKHi{} at $k\!=\!48$ and
$128$ while the control climbs \HzMedCtlKLo{} to \HzMedCtlKHi{}. Of \HzNGen{}
generations \HzExclCap{} hit our budget and \HzExclDegen{} were degenerate,
leaving \HzNCellLo{}--\HzNCellHi{} per cell; dropping truncated items is
conservative, their counts being censored downward.

The controls stop us reading this as counting collapse alone: they saturate too,
so these decoders have a general utterance-length ceiling and the reportable
quantity is the \emph{ratio}, which divides it out. Fitting $\hat c(k)=\hat
K(1-e^{-k/\hat K})$ over the combined ladder --- $\hat K$ a saturation scale read
off counts, \emph{not} the theorem's $N^\ast$, a function of the unmeasured $q$
--- gives $\hat K_{\mathrm{rep}}=\HzNRep{}$ $[\HzNRepLo{},\HzNRepHi{}]$ against
$\hat K_{\mathrm{ctl}}=\HzNCtl{}$ $[\HzNCtlLo{},\HzNCtlHi{}]$: repetition
lowers the counting horizon \HzRatio{}-fold, saturating just past where our
ladder stopped, which is why $k\le32$ looked proportional.

The panel is not unanimous, and the exception is informative: intervals are
disjoint for \HzSepNames{}, while \HzRevNames{} shows \emph{no} repeated-side
saturation within $k\le128$ and inverts the ratio --- the same checkpoint with no
deficit at $k\le32$, a conditional theorem behaving conditionally.

What degrades with $k$ is reliability, not proportion: the exactly-right share
falls from \ExactRepKLo{}\% to \ExactRepKHi{}\% between
$k\!=\!\ExactRepKLoVal{}$ and $\ExactRepKHiVal{}$. Because the claim concerns models rather than our corpus, the checkpoint is the
unit of replication. The exactly-correct rate favours the control in all \CkExactN{} (mean
\CkExact{} points $[\CkExactLo{},\CkExactHi{}]$); the median-error gap is
positive in \CkErrNPos{} of \CkErrN{}, zero in \ErrBestModel{}. Those six
cluster into \FamExactN{} families, so per family the gap is \FamExact{} points,
range $[\FamExactLo{},\FamExactHi{}]$, positive in all \FamExactN{}. At either
level the panel is too small for significance testing --- the exact signed-rank
floor at $n\!=\!6$ is $0.031$ and no multiplicity correction clears $0.05$ (S11)
--- so we rest on effect sizes and their consistency.

\subsection{The limit is periodicity, not length}

Figure~\ref{fig:main}(a) is also the paper's sharpest test. Each control has its
twin's carrier and word count, differing only in that the $k$ copies of one word
become non-adjacent ones. Were the failure about length, attention span or
exposure bias the curves would coincide. They do not: at $k\ge6$ the median
control error is \ErrCtl{}\% $[\ErrCtlLo{},\ErrCtlHi{}]$ ($n=\ErrCtlN{}$), at
every $k$ to $32$ and for every model. The contrast is sharpest
in exactly-correct renderings, \ExactCtl{}\% for controls against
\ExactRep{}\% for their twins: decoders that miscount a repeated sequence five
times in six render its non-adjacent twin right nineteen times in twenty. Controls are not perfect --- \CtlMissPct{}\% carry genuine
truncations --- but they are exact where the repeated items are not.

Above $k\!=\!8$ the control's fillers cycle a pool of eight, making that contrast
period-$1$ against period-$8$. We therefore re-generated the $k=12\ldots32$
controls from a never-cycled $146$-word pool, pairing them with the repeated
items already scored so only the control changes. The dissociation survives at
\ApMidGap{} points (\ApMidRep{}\% against \ApMidCtl{}\%, $n=\ApMidN{}$) where
cycled controls give \ApCycGap{}: the confound is worth \ApCost{} points, not
the bulk of the effect. Improbability and an acoustic attractor fail their own
predictions (S8).

A third rival is a decoding rule rather than a mechanism: the families ship
repetition penalties differing by an order of magnitude, and a penalty suppresses
repeated tokens by construction. It is not the cause. Sweeping XTTS-v2 over a
\PenFold{}-fold penalty range leaves the repeated exact-rate between
\PenRepLo{}\% and \PenRepHi{}\% (\PenSlope{} points per unit over the
\PenArms{} arms whose control survives; at $1.0$ the control itself collapses to
\PenOffCtl{}\%, making that setting unusable rather than informative), and the
\PenNoneN{} Llasa checkpoints pass \emph{no} penalty at all yet show the effect
at full size, \PenNoneRep{}\% against \PenNoneCtl{}\%.

The last rival is architectural, the one the title stakes: perhaps any
synthesiser mishandles long repeated text. The same ladder through
VITS~\cite{kim2021vits}, which has no autoregressive decoder --- a duration
predictor and flow vocoder emit the waveform at once, leaving
Assumption~\ref{ass:periodic} no recurrence to act on --- shows \emph{no}
dissociation: \NonARRep{}\% of repeated items exact against \NonARCtl{}\% of
controls, a gap of \NonARGap{} points where the panel's is $+\ARPoolGap{}$, and
all \NonARAbove{} AR checkpoints separate from it. It degrades with length on
both families alike. This also settles what auditing the recogniser could not:
were blank-collapse manufacturing the gap it would have depressed VITS's repeated
items too, same judge and strings. Being smaller, only its within-model
dissociation is compared.

\subsection{The decoder buys states more slowly under repetition}

Theorem~\ref{thm:collapse}(ii) says states visited under periodic conditioning
stop being mutually distinguishable, so more repetitions should buy distinct
internal states more slowly than non-repetitive text of the same length. Counting
states by the trajectory's effective rank, the capacity gain
$\mathrm{d}\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{eff}}/\mathrm{d}\log k$ on repeated text is a
factor \CapRatio{} of the control's (Figure~\ref{fig:main}(c)), positive in all
\CkCapN{} checkpoints (mean \CkCap{} $[\CkCapLo{},\CkCapHi{}]$) but varying
fourfold: general in direction, not magnitude. Rendering \emph{very} sixteen
times does produce monotonous audio, so the low rank could be the stimulus rather
than lost capacity; covarying out realised output diversity leaves the ratio at
\CapAdjRatio{}, and restricting to correctly rendered items at \CapCorrRatio{}
on a subset that is admittedly not like-for-like. Staying positive, the gain says
repetition slows state acquisition without halting it.

Lemma~\ref{lem:dilution}'s premise holds only approximately
($\delta\le\DeltaMax{}$ nats, S4) and its dose-response prediction fails
outright: within a $(\text{model},k)$ cell, flatter attention goes with
\emph{better} counting ($r=\DilR{}$ $[\DilRLo{},\DilRHi{}]$; S12). We record
that as disconfirming: whatever selects which generations fail is not the degree
of dilution.
